definition: In metaphysics and statistics, a causal model (also called a structural causal model) is a conceptual model that represents the causal mechanisms of a system.
details: Causal models often employ formal causal notation, such as structural equation modeling or causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), to describe relationships among variables and to guide inference. By clarifying which variables should be included, excluded, or controlled for, causal models can improve the design of empirical studies and the interpretation of results. They can also enable researchers to answer some causal questions using observational data, reducing the need for interventional studies such as randomized controlled trials. In cases where randomized experiments are impractical or unethical—for example, when studying the effects of environmental exposures or social determinants of health—causal models provide a framework for drawing valid conclusions from non-experimental data. Causal models can help with the question of external validity (whether results from one study apply to unstudied populations). Causal models can allow data from multiple studies to be merged (in certain circumstances) to answer questions that cannot be answered by any individual data set. explainer.lead: A causal model is a map of how one thing can bring about another, rather than just a record of things that occur together. It helps researchers decide what to measure and control for, and can sometimes support causal conclusions when experiments are impractical or unethical.

tiers.eli5: Imagine drawing arrows to show what makes what happen: rain makes the pavement wet, and wet pavement can make someone slip. A causal model is that kind of map, used to work out whether changing one thing would change another. It also helps researchers avoid being fooled by other factors that affect both.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners express assumptions with causal directed acyclic graphs or structural equation models, then use them to choose adjustment variables and interpret estimates. These models are especially useful for observational epidemiology and for assessing whether findings transfer to new populations or can be combined across studies. The main pitfall is treating the chosen graph as proven: an unsupported causal structure or inappropriate control variable can produce misleading conclusions.
tiers.paperLevel: A structural causal model represents causal mechanisms among variables, commonly using a causal DAG or structural equations. In plain-text DAG notation, an edge X -> Y encodes a proposed direct causal relationship; the resulting structure guides identification and adjustment for observational inference. Causal conclusions depend on the model's assumptions, while transport to unstudied populations and merging multiple data sets are possible only in certain circumstances.

explainer.example: To study whether an environmental exposure causes a health outcome, a researcher might draw arrows from the exposure to the outcome and from a social determinant of health to both. The model identifies that determinant as a variable to control for when estimating the exposure's effect from observational data. This is useful when randomly assigning people to the exposure would be unethical.

explainer.intuition: Correlation says that variables move together; a causal model adds an explicit account of which mechanisms could produce that pattern. Its arrows and equations make assumptions visible so researchers can reason about interventions, confounding, and study design.
howItWorks: Identify the variables and the causal question.
Represent proposed mechanisms with structural equations or a causal DAG.
Use the structure to decide which variables to include, exclude, or control for.
Where the assumptions permit, estimate causal effects from observational data or assess whether results transfer across populations.
explainer.whyItMatters: Causal models can improve empirical study design and the interpretation of results, and can reduce reliance on randomized controlled trials when their assumptions support observational inference. They also provide a framework for external validity and, in certain circumstances, for combining studies to answer questions no single data set can answer.
misconceptions: Drawing an arrow does not establish that the causal relationship is real; it records an assumption or hypothesis.
Controlling for more variables is not always better—the causal structure should guide the choice.
Observational data do not automatically yield causal answers, and causal models do not make every experiment unnecessary.
